sections.heading: What is a nasal vowel?
sections.body:
In a nasal vowel, air goes out through the nose and the mouth at the same time. The **n** or **m** after the vowel is not pronounced as a consonant — it only tells you the vowel is nasal. Standard French has three nasal vowels you must tell apart:

(Many speakers in the south of France, and older speakers, keep a fourth one, [œ̃], in *un* and *brun*. In most of France today it sounds like [ɛ̃].)

head: Sound
Usual spellings
Examples
rows: in, im, ain, ein, un, yn

sections.heading: Hearing the difference
sections.body:
These words differ only in their nasal vowel — listen to each several times:

- *vent* [vɑ̃] (wind) — *vont* [vɔ̃] (they go) — *vin* [vɛ̃] (wine)
- *lent* [lɑ̃] (slow) — *long* [lɔ̃] (long) — *lin* [lɛ̃] (linen)
- *temps* [tɑ̃] (time, weather) — *ton* [tɔ̃] (your) — *thym* [tɛ̃] (thyme)

Tip: for [ɑ̃] open your mouth wide; for [ɔ̃] round your lips; for [ɛ̃] spread your lips as for a smile.

sections.heading: When the vowel is NOT nasal
sections.body:
The vowel is **oral** (not nasal) when the n or m is doubled or followed by a vowel — then you hear the n or m:

- *bon* [bɔ̃] — *bonne* [bɔn]
- *an* [ɑ̃] — *année* [a.ne]
- *plein* [plɛ̃] — *pleine* [plɛn]
- *américain* [a.me.ʁi.kɛ̃] — *américaine* [a.me.ʁi.kɛn]

This is exactly what happens with many feminine forms.

examples: Il y a du vent aujourd'hui.
Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
A glass of red wine, please.
Je mange du pain le matin.
I eat bread in the morning.
Je n'ai pas le temps maintenant.
